dossier.public_summary: The dip alternates between shallow (~160 ppm) and deep (~577 ppm) every orbit, which is expected for a binary eclipse folded at the wrong period. Depths also change from sector to sector and from transit to transit, with two transits much deeper than the rest. The shape is V-like and grazing, not the flat bottom expected for a 1.8 Earth-radius planet. Together this is best explained by an eclipsing binary, not a planet.

reasons.why: Odd and even events differ at >5 sigma and by a factor of ~3.6, which is far beyond measurement errors for a bright (Tmag=8.729) star. This is the classic signature of a signal at half the true orbital period, i.e. an eclipsing binary alternating between deep and shallow eclipses.

Depth changes dramatically within the same SPOC pipeline, not because of calibration between products. An astrophysical change with sector/aperture argues against a stable planet transit and supports a blend/variable-depth binary.

reasons.why: Individual transit depths are wildly inconsistent, with the signal dominated (94% of chi2) by two anomalously deep events. This is not consistent with a single transiting planet with stable depth.

reasons.why: Transit shape is V-shaped and near-grazing with very high impact parameter and a transit that is inconsistent with the stellar density. A flat-bottomed planet is disfavoured; a grazing stellar binary can mimic this shape.
ML planet rank is in the false-positive regime, consistent with the combined odd-even and sector/transit depth variability evidence.
